newsitem.title: CZECH REPUBLIC: Albright sees proof of relatives' Holocaust death.
newsitem.headline: Albright sees proof of relatives' Holocaust death.

text.p: U.S. Secretary of State Madeleine Albright came home to her native Prague on Sunday to confront for the first time painful evidence that two of her grandparents perished in the Nazi Holocaust.
After seeing their names inscribed on a wall in the Czech capital's Pinkas synagogue, she said in an emotional statement that the image "will forever be seared into my heart".

Albright, brought up a Roman Catholic by her parents who fled the Nazi invasion of Czechoslovakia, has said she only learned for sure of her Jewish background and the fate of her grandparents from a Washington Post article earlier this year.

She flew to the Czech Republic on Sunday as part of a Central and East European tour to explain NATO's expansion policy, but took time off from official duties to explore Prague's Jewish cemetery, synagogue and the town hall of the city's old Jewish quarter.

Speaking on a dark and narrow street outside the town hall, she said she had never thought to look for her grandparents' names during previous visits to the synagogue, where the names of more than 77,000 Czech Holocaust victims are recorded.
"Tonight, I knew to look for those names," she said.

A card index she was shown recorded that her paternal grandparents, Arnost and Olga Korbel, were sent to Terezin concentration camp near Prague in July 1942. Arnost died there soon afterwards while Olga is believed to have died at Auschwitz camp in Poland in 1944.
Albright and her parents spent the war in England, then returned to Czechoslovakia, only to leave again for the United States in 1948 when communists took control of their country.

Her voice breaking with emotion, Albright said that in leaving family members behind when they fled the Nazis, her parents "confronted the most excruciating decision a human being can face... even as they saved me from certain death".

Her new awareness of her Jewish background meant that "the evil of the Holocaust has an even more personal meaning for me, and I feel an even greater determination to ensure that it will never be forgotten", Albright said.
After reading her prepared statement, Albright turned and strode away up the street, as security men kept reporters away. "Her view was that this was an intensely personal issue," a spokesman said.

Her pilgrimage to the Jewish monuments of Prague capped a day which began with talks in St Petersburg with Russian Foreign Minister Yevgeny Primakov and continued with a five-and-a-half-hour visit to the Lithuanian capital Vilnius.
In Vilnius, Albright ignored Russian objections to tell the three Baltic states that they were "serious candidates... on the road" to NATO membership.

She sought to reassure Estonia, Latvia and Lithuania that Washington supported their eventual membership even though a NATO summit last week gave no indication when they might to be invited to join the alliance.

But after talks with Baltic foreign ministers, she also made clear that if the three states were to join NATO they must improve ties with Russia, including through their treatment of Russian minorities.
The NATO summit in Madrid invited Poland, the Czech Republic and Hungary to become the first ex-communist countries to apply to join the alliance.

The Baltic states were forced into the Soviet Union during World War Two and became independent in 1991. Still fearful for their freedom, the three countries are anxious to gain the protection of NATO membership as soon as possible.
But Russia has said it may tear up a recently signed charter of cooperation with NATO if former Soviet republics are admitted to the alliance.
"We must continue to make clear that NATO enlargement is not directed at Russia -- and you must help us," Albright said in a speech at Vilnius University.
"This process is not about escaping west, it is about gaining the confidence to look to the east in a spirit of cooperation."

Earlier, U.S. officials said she and Primakov had agreed to seek an extension of 30-nation talks in Vienna on updating a European conventional arms treaty in a bid to reach a framework agreement by the end of July.

The current round of the talks is about to end, but a senior U.S. official said Albright and Primakov would jointly recommend to the negotiators to stay in session to try to reach an outline deal on the Conventional Forces in Europe pact.
